title: QUIC and HTTP/3 behind ZIA: where it escapes and how to block it

prose.text: QUIC (HTTP/3 over UDP, see [[zia.saas-apps]] for the other causes) is the reason an app can seem to ignore SSL inspection: SSL/TLS Inspection needs TCP session information, and QUIC does not use TCP. The headline fact, that Zscaler recommends blocking QUIC so the browser falls back to TCP, is in [[zia.ssl-inspection.uninspectable]]. {{cert-errors}}
How to block it depends on how the traffic reaches Zscaler ([[zia.firewall.traffic-path]] covers the firewall path).

cert-errors.statement: Zscaler cannot examine QUIC sessions when SSL/TLS Inspection is on, and users may also see certificate errors when QUIC is used.

quotes: Because of this, Zscaler cannot examine QUIC sessions when users have SSL/TLS Inspection enabled. When using QUIC, users might also experience certificate errors.

tunnel2-firewall-rule.statement: For traffic arriving through a GRE or IPSec tunnel, or Client Connector with Z-Tunnel 2.0, QUIC is blocked with a Firewall Filtering rule on the QUIC network service, which forces the browser back to TCP 80 and 443. Z-Tunnel 2.0 can send all ports and protocols.

quotes: you can effectively block QUIC by creating a Firewall Filtering rule. This blocks QUIC UDP flows and forces the browser to default to TCP 80/443.
As configured in the following steps, the Firewall Filtering rule blocks QUIC at the network service level.
Click the Services tab and select QUIC under Network Services.
Z-Tunnel 2.0 is capable of sending all ports and protocols.

default-rule-blocks.statement: The default Firewall Filtering rule (lowest rank) normally blocks QUIC unless it is specifically allowed, but admin-created permissive rules above it often let QUIC through, so a QUIC block rule may need to precede them.

quotes: Normally, the default Firewall Filtering Rule (the lowest rank rule) blocks QUIC unless specifically allowed.

However, admins often create more general connectivity rules or groups of rules (e.g., User X or Source IP Address Y to Destination Group IP Address Y is allowed) that are overly permissive and do not explicitly exclude the use of QUIC.
For this reason, one or more QUIC block rules might be needed to precede admin-defined allow rules.

udp-80.statement: QUIC can use UDP destination port 80 as well as 443, so to include port 80 in the QUIC network service, the predefined network service can be modified or a custom network service configured.

quotes: In addition to UDP destination port 443, QUIC can use UDP destination port 80.
To include port 80 in the network service definition of QUIC, you can modify the predefined network service or configure a custom network service.

tunnel1-device-firewall.statement: For Client Connector traffic on Z-Tunnel 1.0 (which sends all proxy-aware traffic or port 80 and 443 traffic, depending on the forwarding profile configuration), the block belongs on the device firewall: UDP 80 and 443.

quotes: If you are only sending Zscaler Client Connector traffic that uses Z-Tunnel 1.0 to Zscaler (or leveraging remote users), create a block rule on your device firewall to block UDP 80 and 443.
Z-Tunnel 1.0 sends all proxy-aware traffic or port 80/443 traffic to the Zscaler service, depending on the forwarding profile configuration.

tunnel1-udp-leaves.statement: So under Z-Tunnel 1.0, or any TCP 80 and 443 only forwarding, QUIC UDP does not reach Zscaler at all: it leaves the device directly and is neither inspected nor blocked by a Zscaler Firewall Filtering rule.
tunnel1-udp-leaves.conditions: Inference from Help directing the block to the device or branch firewall; the legacy phrasing "egresses outside the tunnel" is not in a source.

tcp-only-branch.statement: If only TCP 80 and 443 go over the tunnel to Zscaler, QUIC is blocked on the branch firewall.

quotes: If you are only sending TCP 80/443 over a tunnel to Zscaler, block QUIC on your branch firewall.

dns-https-records.statement: QUIC can also be discouraged with a DNS Control rule that blocks the HTTPS resource record type with a Server Failure response, because browsers use those records to choose HTTP/3 and the Zscaler web proxy currently does not support HTTP/3.

quotes: Additionally, you can manage QUIC using the DNS Control policy by blocking the HTTPS DNS resource record type.
HTTPS records are increasingly used by web browsers and applications to leverage the use of HTTP/3 with QUIC, which the Zscaler web proxy currently does not support.
Zscaler recommends configuring your DNS Control policy to block HTTPS resource records to suppress the use of HTTP/3 over QUIC
This rule configuration blocks HTTPS resource records and sends a Server Failure response (i.e., ServFail DNS response code per RFC 6895) to the client.

conferencing-media.title: Webex and Teams media over Z-Tunnel 2.0 and process-based bypass
conferencing-media.detail: Unverified legacy statement: "The canonical case where this matters: WebEx media (UDP 9000 SRTP, fallback TCP 443) and Microsoft Teams call quality. If Z-Tunnel 2.0 captures the media flow, voice/video degrades. Process-based bypass of the conferencing client is the documented pattern." The captured Z-Tunnel and QUIC pages do not mention Webex or Teams media; the captured Advanced Policy Settings page covers a UCaaS One Click option for Zoom, GoTo, RingCentral, Webex and Talkdesk, not Teams media.
